doc.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001

title: Trombone influences: Louis Armstrong and the plunger players, Teagarden, Wells and others
summary: Gordon names Louis Armstrong as his greatest influence and lists trombonists he studied, including Teagarden, Trummy Young, Al Grey, Watrous, J.J. Johnson, Lawrence Brown and Tyree Glenn.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Right. Who were your major trombone influences?

I know this doesn’t answer your question, I think my greatest influence was not a trombone player, it was Louis Armstrong actually. But guys that played with him. I’m often asked the question who is my favorite. I don’t really have one favorite because the trombone has many voices. And you have people like Jack Teagarden or Trummy Young, guys like Al Grey. Even guys like Frank Rosolino. A guy like Bill Watrous. I admired Bill Watrous for a long time. I got a chance to hear him when I was in high school and started to develop my playing I heard a recording of him and I was like man, okay. Trombone? And then you know I got a chance to meet him and play with him live. Who else? I mean I like guys like Vic Dickenson and Dicky Wells because of how they used the trombone. I mean you have guys that played plunger and there’s so many differences between the way Al Grey plays or the way that Tricky Sam Nanton plays, all the way to Bubber Miley plays plunger, the difference between him and Cootie Williams. And they’re trumpet players, but just speaking a little bit about the plunger, there are so many guys. I love Slide Hampton. I wouldn’t say that he was a traditional, traditional as

is categorized with the early New Orleans style or even a Dixieland style. I love J.J. Johnson. He’s great. He’s one of the cleanest trombone players ever. I love Curtis Fuller. I got a chance to work with him a couple of weeks ago. There are many. Major influences? I say guys like Lawrence Brown. He played the trombone like a trombone. He didn’t try to do the acrobatics of a saxophone or a trumpet. He played the trombone. He sang. He sang when he played. A lot of guys. Britt Woodman even. Some of the guys, well he’s no longer with us, but Buster Cooper, the way he played trombone. He will, when he wants to, he can play pretty sweet but when he wants to man just fly, he like whip.
Do they call him the bumble bee or something?

I guess. But I mean and one of the great things about, I didn’t get a chance to meet all of these guys, but their personalities are just so great, they’re great people. Like I said Louis Armstrong is my, I would say is my, the one, if I had to choose one person that was most influential in jazz slash music to me I would have to say it was Louis Armstrong. But guys that played with him, Quentin “Butter” Jackson. I know he was another great trombone player. And he was also another one of the great plunger mute men. The guy that played vibes — I can never think of his name and he played with Pops, he played with Duke, and he was a great vibraphonist.

Hmmm? Not Slide. It’s not Al Grey, I can’t think of it. It’s going to come to me in a second. Oh, Tyree Glenn. I can never think of why I always get tied up with his name, Tyree. He played with Louis Armstrong. He was a great trombonist also. And I called all of those names, I think they all influenced me because at one point I spent time studying their style of playing or a particular solo that they may have done. Like the difference between the way Al Grey plays plunger, the way Tyree plays, the way that Quentin “Butter” Jackson plays. The way that Tricky Sam Nanton plays. You have a different approach to the plunger. And I listened to all of those. Open horn, the guys that played with Louis Armstrong. With Jack Teagarden. I love Jack Teagarden. He’s great. I mean he had great command and mastery of the instrument. But he played a little different from Trummy Young but I like both of their styles. Vic Dickinson and Dicky Wells. You listen to them play sometimes and you just want to start laughing. Because when they play they kind of had a human element in the — a vocal element when they played on some of the recordings that I’ve heard. I heard one recording of — I can’t think of the name of the recording but it was a comedy show. And they were playing. And Vic Dickinson? Dicky — it was one of them. And they started off their thing like [scats] it was just like someone saying something. And it was just — I said oh man.
